Ultimate total length in the Wels catfish reaches an extraordinary 278 centimeters [Li = 278 centimeters], making this European species one of the largest freshwater teleosts globally. At hatching, free-swimming larvae emerge from their adhesive eggs at a total length of just 0.7 centimeters [Lb = 0.7 centimeters], a remarkable size disparity that reflects an extreme ontogenetic trajectory. The wet weight at birth is correspondingly minute, with prolarvae weighing approximately 0.0012 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0012 grams] when the chorion ruptures and the yolk-sac larva enters its lecithotrophic phase. During the first week of development at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the larval body plan reorganises rapidly, culminating in the onset of exogenous feeding after an age at birth of 7 days [ab = 7 days] from fertilisation. This period of yolk absorption and fin differentiation sets the stage for a growth trajectory that will eventually produce the massive asymptotic body mass characteristic of the species.

Female Wels catfish attain puberty at a total length of 87.5 centimeters [Lp = 87.5 centimeters], a size threshold that triggers the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis. This represents a substantial early investment in somatic growth before reproductive activation begins. The wet weight at puberty for females is recorded at 4500 grams [Wwp = 4500 grams], reflecting the considerable body mass required to support the energetic demands of egg production in this iteroparous species. Field studies employing otolith microchemistry and mark-recapture data indicate that, under the thermal regime characteristic of temperate European waters (20 °C [T = 20 °C]), the time since birth at puberty is 2355 days [tp = 2355 days]. Puberty thus occurs after approximately six and a half years of growth, during which the fish transitions from a planktonic larva through larval metamorphosis to a benthic juvenile and ultimately to a reproductively viable post-pubertal adult.

The ultimate wet weight of the Wels catfish has been documented at 114000 grams [Wwi = 114000 grams] from large-scale fishery surveys across the Danube and Volga river basins. This massive adult body mass, corresponding to over 110 kilograms, represents the culmination of decades of continuous feeding and growth in productive floodplain habitats. Such extreme dimensions position Silurus glanis as a clear outlier among European freshwater fishes, exceeding even large pike and sturgeon species in maximum recorded body mass. The transition from a 0.0012 gram hatchling to a 114 kilogram adult constitutes a weight increase spanning eight orders of magnitude, a life-history strategy predicated on high initial fecundity and low juvenile survival rates. Adults exhibit a benthic foraging ecology, consuming a broad diet ranging from benthic macroinvertebrates to fish and occasional waterbirds, which fuels the sustained growth required to approach this enormous asymptotic mass.

Under the thermal conditions typical of mid-latitude populations (20 °C [T = 20 °C]), the maximum recorded longevity for the Wels catfish is 29200 days [am = 29200 days]. This extreme lifespan, among the longest documented for any freshwater teleost, is supported by low natural mortality rates once individuals exceed a body length of around 100 centimeters and attain a broad gape that minimises predation risk. The reproductive schedule of this species is correspondingly slow: females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], and each spawning event yields approximately 3,420,000 eggs [N_R_i = each spawning event yields approximately 3,420,000 eggs] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This annual reproductive investment, calculated from extensive gill-net surveys of gravid females during the spring spawning migration, underscores a life-history strategy that prioritises somatic growth and extended lifespan above high annual fecundity.

The Wels catfish reaches an ultimate total length of 278 centimeters [Li = 278 centimeters], placing it among the largest freshwater teleosts. Post-larval transformation and the pelagic-benthic transition occur within the first growing season, with juveniles recruiting to benthic habitats at lengths of 15 to 25 centimeters. The maximum daily reproduction rate reaches approximately 9370 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 9370 eggs per day]. Comparative analyses with other large-bodied silurids, such as the Mekong giant catfish Pangasianodon gigas, reveal that the Wels catfish exhibits a substantially slower growth trajectory but a greater ultimate body length, suggesting fundamental differences in metabolic scaling and resource allocation strategies between these two apex predators. The species' extreme longevity and deferred reproduction represent a classic bet-hedging strategy adapted to variable floodplain environments.
